results.summary_before: This is a standalone VGA demo that renders a Matrix-style digital rain animation using glyphs, with four selectable VGA timing modes and two palette selection pins. It requires the TinyVGA PMOD and a pixel clock near 25.175 MHz for the default mode, with higher resolutions requiring correspondingly higher clocks and mode pin settings. Silicon test reports from both the author and an independent tester confirm that the video modes, color palettes, mode inputs, and reset all work, including 1024x768 at 60 to 70 Hz. The design is notable for being verified across multiple resolutions on real hardware.

results.summary_before: This project implements a numerically controlled oscillator with linear-interpolated sine output. It uses an 8-bit frequency control input and produces an 8-bit DAC output, with a 16-bit phase accumulator and sine ROM with interpolation. The design is a basic block for direct digital synthesis and requires an external 8-bit DAC and oscilloscope for testing. It is a compact and efficient NCO suitable for generating sine waves with controlled frequency.

results.summary_before: This design drives a 640x480 VGA output showing a bouncing Zero to ASIC logo, with options for tiled mode and an animated colour gradient. It is tested by connecting a VGA monitor and setting the tile and solid-colour inputs, and an optional Gamepad Pmod can start, pause and steer the logo. External hardware is the Tiny VGA Pmod and optionally the Gamepad Pmod. A silicon test report confirms it works after setting the clock, making it a verified VGA animation design.

results.summary_before: This design displays a large 480x480 pixel Tiny Tapeout logo over VGA using time-based dithering to extend the apparent color range. It drives the standard TinyVGA PMOD pinout with two bits per color channel plus HSync and VSync, and runs from a 25.175 MHz clock. It is used simply by connecting a VGA monitor through the TinyVGA PMOD and powering the chip. Silicon test reports confirm it works on multiple boards, including at 32 MHz, with testers noting the dithering makes the image slightly fuzzy but yields an impressive color range.

results.summary_before: The E-Beam Inspection Pixel Core processes 8-bit pixel data at one pixel per cycle, computing a running mean using an IIR filter, local contrast, and edge magnitude. It outputs defect flags and a 4-bit magnitude nibble, and can be configured via a tiny SPI interface. The core is designed for integration into larger inspection systems and requires no external hardware for basic operation. The documentation describes the functionality and interface but does not provide specific testing procedures or silicon results.

results.summary_before: This is a rudimentary implementation of the popular 2013 bird-flapping game, rendered over VGA. One input makes the bird go up and another starts the game, with output through a standard Tiny VGA pinout. A VGA Pmod is needed for video output, and a Python reference implementation is provided for comparison. The documentation notes that the reference and actual implementations have inputs offset by one cycle.
